newsitem.title: PARAGUAY: Paraguayan industry minister resigns over scandal.
newsitem.headline: Paraguayan industry minister resigns over scandal.

text.p: Paraguayan Industry and Trade Minister Ubaldo Scavone resigned on Monday for "ethical reasons" over a financial scandal that has shaken the banking system and plunged the government into crisis.

Scavone had been accused of covering up financial problems at the biggest private bank in Paraguay, Banco Union, which is controlled by his family, and was under pressure to quit from the ruling Colorado Party.
He is the first political victim since the government acknowledged that as early as two years ago it learned of irregularities in banks it took control of because of liquidity problems on June 16.
Presidential Chief of Staff Miguel Ramirez told reporters Scavone submitted his "irrevocable resignation for ethical reasons that impede him from continuing at the helm of the portfolio."
Scavone was the longest-serving member of the Cabinet and took office along with President Juan Carlos Wasmosy in 1993.

He is the brother of the former president of Banco Union. Shortly before taking it over on June 16, central bank authorities detected bank executives had used some government financial aid for personal use.
Last February the Controller General, who supervises the spending of public funds, accused Scavone of covering up the bank's problems because of his family's majority stake in the institution.

Last week, Paraguay's Congress and the leadership of the ruling Colorado Party demanded the resignation of the whole economic cabinet, comprising the ministers of finance, industry, agriculture and public works as well as the central bank chief.

Wasmosy, who was elected in 1993 with about 47 percent of the vote, has been increasingly isolated. A dissident wing took control of the Colorado Party last year and his vice-president, Roberto Seifart, has become highly critical of Wasmosy's policies.
Authorities also took control of Banco Inversiones and Ahorros Paraguayos, a savings and loan institution with links to Banco Union.
The central bank is committed by law to guarantee deposits of up to $2,300. About 50 percent of depositors had greater investments than that in Banco Union.
The International Monetary Fund and Inter-American Development Bank have offered their assistance to stem the banking crisis and suggested urgent action to strengthen the system.
